claims.text: Living standards are the level of material well-being of a person or a household - how well the household is housed, fed, clothed, schooled and cared for - together with the security of that level.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Gross Domestic Product is the total value of the goods and services produced in a country in a given period; GDP per head is that total divided by the population, so it shows the average output available per person and is the figure to compare living standards between countries or over time.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The indicators that complete the picture of living standards are: income per person, health measures such as life expectancy and infant mortality, education measures such as mean years of schooling and literacy, and access to basic services such as clean water and electricity; taken together they capture what GDP per head alone may miss.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: GDP per head is an average, so it may hide differences: where income is spread unevenly, the typical household may earn well below the average, and output may include goods that change living standards little, which is why the wider indicators are read alongside it.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: To compare living standards between countries, GDP per head is adjusted for the cost of living in each country and read alongside health, education and access indicators, because a money figure alone may mislead where prices differ.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The distribution of income is how a country's total income is shared among its households; living standards depend not just on the average income the country produces but on where a household sits in that sharing.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Two countries with the same GDP per head may keep different living standards where their income is shared differently: where income is spread more evenly, a typical household is likely to live better than in a country of equal average income where a small group takes the larger share.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A progressive income tax takes a larger share of income from high earners than from low earners, so it tends to narrow the gap in take-home income; a regressive income tax takes a larger share from low earners than from high earners, so it tends to widen the gap. The test that tells them apart is which group pays the larger share of its own income, not which group pays the larger amount.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Real GDP is GDP measured at constant prices, that is, adjusted for changes in the price level, so it changes only when the quantity of goods and services produced changes; real GDP per head is real GDP divided by the population, the average real output per person.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Real GDP per head has advantages as a measure of living standards: the data are collected regularly in most countries, the adjustment for inflation lets years be compared fairly, the division by population lets countries of different sizes be compared, and a higher figure means more goods and services are available per person on average.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Real GDP per head may hide inequality, unpaid household services, working conditions and environmental damage. Own-consumption crops and self-built housing are included in GDP in principle, but subsistence and informal production can be difficult to measure and may be under-recorded. International comparisons also require adjustment for differences in purchasing power.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The Human Development Index (HDI) is a measure of living standards published each year by the United Nations Development Programme that combines three components into one number between 0 and 1: health, measured by life expectancy at birth; education, measured by mean years of schooling of adults and expected years of schooling of children starting school; and income, measured by GNI per head at purchasing power parity (PPP). A figure closer to 1 means higher human development.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The HDI's advantages are that it is broader than an income measure, capturing health and education outcomes, and that its income component is adjusted for the cost of living; its disadvantages are that it is still a national average that may hide inequality between regions and groups, that it leaves out other parts of living standards such as freedom, housing, working conditions and the environment, that years of schooling say little about the quality of learning, and that its data may be estimated or out of date in some countries.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Living standards tend to differ between countries because of differences in productivity (the capital, skills and technology each worker has to work with), in natural resources, in the growth of population relative to output, in education and healthcare, in the share of workers in low-productivity farming, in saving and investment, and in political stability and infrastructure.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Living standards and income tend to differ within a country because workers hold different skills and qualifications and so earn different wages, because wealth such as land, property and shares is unevenly owned and earns rent, interest, dividends and profit, because some people are unemployed or too old or ill to work, because well-paid jobs and services tend to cluster in cities and some regions, and because the tax and benefit system may narrow or widen the gap.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.
